paragraphs: It is clear that the southernmost States of the Union cannot abolish slavery without running very great dangers, ones the North had no reason to fear when it freed its Black population. We have already described how the Northern States manage the transition from slavery to freedom: they keep the present generation in chains and set their descendants free. In this way Black people are brought into society gradually. While the men who might abuse their freedom remain in servitude, those who are freed can learn the art of being free before they become their own masters. But this method would be hard to apply in the South. To declare that all Black children born after a certain date shall be free is to introduce the principle and the idea of liberty into the heart of slavery. The Black people whom the law keeps enslaved, while their children are released from that condition, are astonished at so unequal a fate, and their astonishment is only the prelude to impatience and resentment. From then on, slavery loses in their eyes the kind of moral power it drew from time and habit; it is reduced to a plain abuse of force. The Northern States had nothing to fear from this contrast, because Black people there were few and the white population was very large. But if this faint dawn of freedom were to show two million men their true position, the oppressors would have reason to tremble. Once they had freed the children of their slaves, the Europeans of the Southern States would very soon be obliged to extend the same benefit to the entire Black population.

In the North, as I have already remarked, a twofold migration follows the abolition of slavery, or even precedes it when circumstances have made abolition likely. The slaves leave the country to be transported southward, and the whites of the Northern States, along with emigrants from Europe, hurry to fill their place. But these two causes cannot work in the same way in the Southern States. On the one hand, the mass of slaves is too great for anyone to expect that they could ever be removed from the country. On the other hand, the Europeans and the Anglo-Americans of the North are afraid to settle in a country where labor has not yet been restored to its rightful honor. Besides, they very justly regard the States in which Black people equal or outnumber whites as exposed to very great dangers, and they refrain from directing their energies there.

Thus the people of the South could not, like their Northern countrymen, introduce the slaves gradually to freedom by abolishing slavery. They have no way of noticeably reducing the Black population, and they would be left without support to restrain its excesses. So within a few years a great population of free Black people would exist in the heart of a white nation of equal size.

The same abuses of power that still sustain slavery would then become the source of the most alarming perils the white population of the South might have to fear. At present the descendants of the Europeans are the sole owners of the land, the absolute masters of all labor, and the only people who possess wealth, knowledge, and arms. The Black man has none of these advantages, but he gets by without them because he is a slave. If he were free and had to provide for his own subsistence, would it be possible for him to go without these things and still stay alive? Or would not the very instruments of the white man’s present superiority, while slavery lasts, expose him to a thousand dangers if slavery were abolished?

As long as the Black man remains a slave, he can be kept in a condition not very far from that of the animals. But with his liberty he cannot fail to acquire enough instruction to appreciate his misfortunes and to see a remedy for them. Moreover, there is a peculiar principle of relative justice that is very firmly planted in the human heart. People are struck much more forcibly by inequalities within the same class than by those between different classes. It is easier for them to accept slavery than to allow several million citizens to live under a load of eternal infamy and hereditary wretchedness. In the North the population of freed Black people feels these hardships and resents these indignities, but its numbers and its power are small; in the South it would be numerous and strong.

Once it is admitted that whites and emancipated Black people live on the same territory as two foreign communities, it is easy to see that the future holds only two alternatives: Black people and whites must either separate completely or mingle completely. I have already stated my conviction about the latter. *r I do not imagine that the white and Black races will ever live on an equal footing in any country. But I believe the difficulty to be even greater in the United States than elsewhere. An isolated individual may overcome the prejudices of religion, of country, or of race, and if that individual is a king he may bring about surprising changes in society; but a whole people cannot rise, as it were, above itself. A despot who made the Americans and their former slaves bear the same yoke might perhaps succeed in blending their races. But as long as the American democracy remains at the head of affairs, no one will undertake so difficult a task, and it can be foreseen that the freer the white population of the United States becomes, the more isolated it will remain. *s

r [ This opinion is backed by authorities infinitely weightier than anything I can say. For instance, the “Memoirs of Jefferson” (as collected by M. Conseil) state: “Nothing is more clearly written in the book of destiny than the emancipation of the blacks; and it is equally certain that the two races will never live in a state of equal freedom under the same government, so insurmountable are the barriers which nature, habit, and opinions have established between them.”]
s [ If the British West India planters had governed themselves, they would certainly not have passed the Slave Emancipation Bill that the mother country has recently imposed on them.]

I have observed earlier that the mixed race is the true bond of union between the Europeans and the Native Americans. In the same way, people of mixed race are the true means of transition between the white and the Black man, so that wherever they are numerous, the intermixture of the two races is not impossible. In some parts of America the European and Black races have crossed so much that it is rare to meet a man who is entirely Black or entirely white. When they have reached this point, the two races may truly be said to be combined, or rather to have been absorbed into a third race, which is connected with both without being identical with either.

Of all the Europeans, the English are the ones who have mixed least with Black people. More people of mixed race are seen in the South of the Union than in the North, but they are still infinitely scarcer than in any other European colony. They are by no means numerous in the United States; they have no strength of their own, and when quarrels arising from differences of color break out, they generally side with the whites, just as the lackeys of the great in Europe take on the contemptuous airs of the nobility toward the lower orders.

The pride of origin natural to the English is singularly increased by the personal pride that democratic liberty fosters among the Americans. The white citizen of the United States is proud of his race and proud of himself. But if whites and Black people do not intermingle in the North of the Union, how would they mix in the South? Can anyone suppose for a moment that an American of the Southern States, placed as he must forever be between the white man with all his physical and moral superiority and the Black man, will ever think of preferring the latter? The Americans of the Southern States have two powerful passions that will always keep them apart: the first is the fear of being made like Black people, their former slaves; the second is the dread of sinking below the whites, their neighbors.

If I were asked to predict what will probably happen at some future time, I would say that the abolition of slavery in the South will, in the ordinary course of things, increase the white population’s repugnance toward people of color. I base this opinion on a similar observation I had already made in the North. I noticed there that the white inhabitants of the North avoid Black people with increasing care as the legal barriers of separation are removed by the legislature. Why should the same result not occur in the South? In the North, whites are deterred from mixing with Black people by fear of an imaginary danger; in the South, where the danger would be real, I cannot imagine that the fear would be less widespread.

Suppose, on the one hand, it is admitted (and the fact is unquestionable) that the Black population keeps accumulating in the extreme South and that it increases more rapidly than the white population. Suppose, on the other hand, it is granted that no one can foresee a time when whites and Black people will be so intermingled as to draw the same benefits from society. Must we not conclude that Black people and whites will sooner or later come to open conflict in the Southern States of the Union? But if one asks what the outcome of the struggle is likely to be, it is easy to see that we can form only a very vague guess at the truth. The human mind may succeed in drawing a wide circle, as it were, that includes the course of future events; but within that circle a thousand different chances and circumstances may steer it in as many different directions, and every picture of the future contains a dim spot that the eye of the understanding cannot penetrate. It appears, however, extremely probable that in the West Indian Islands the white race is destined to be overcome, and the Black population on the continent to share the same fate.

In the West India Islands the white planters are surrounded by an immense Black population. On the continent, Black people are placed between the ocean and an innumerable people that already spreads over them in a dense mass, from the icy borders of Canada to the frontiers of Virginia, and from the banks of the Missouri to the shores of the Atlantic. If the white citizens of North America remain united, we cannot suppose that Black people will escape the destruction that threatens them; they must be subdued by want or by the sword. But the Black population accumulated along the coast of the Gulf of Mexico has a chance of success if the American Union is dissolved when the struggle between the two races begins. If the federal tie were broken, the citizens of the South would be wrong to rely on any lasting help from their Northern countrymen. The Northerners know well that the danger can never reach them, and unless they are compelled to march to the South’s assistance by a formal obligation, it can be foreseen that the sympathy of color will not be enough to spur them to effort.

Yet whenever the conflict may break out, the whites of the South, even if left to their own resources, will enter the contest with an immense superiority in knowledge and in the means of warfare. But Black people will have numerical strength and the energy of despair on their side, and these are powerful resources for men who have taken up arms. The fate of the white population of the Southern States will perhaps be like that of the Moors in Spain. After occupying the land for centuries, it will perhaps be forced to withdraw to the country its ancestors came from, and to leave to Black people the possession of a territory that Providence seems to have destined more particularly for them, since they can live and work in it more easily than whites.

The danger of a conflict between the white and Black inhabitants of the Southern States of the Union — a danger that, however remote, is inevitable — haunts the imagination of the Americans without rest. The people of the North make it a common topic of conversation, although they have no direct injury to fear from the struggle, but they try in vain to devise some means of avoiding the misfortunes they foresee. In the Southern States the subject is not discussed. The planter does not mention the future when talking with strangers; the citizen does not share his apprehensions with his friends; he tries to hide them from himself. But there is something more alarming in the silent forebodings of the South than in the loud fears of the Northern States.

This all-pervading anxiety has given birth to an undertaking that is little known but may change the fate of a portion of the human race. Out of apprehension of the dangers I have just described, a certain number of American citizens have formed a society to export to the coast of Guinea, at their own expense, any free Black people who are willing to escape the oppression to which they are subject. *t In 1820 the society I am speaking of founded a settlement in Africa, at the seventh degree of north latitude, which bears the name of Liberia. The most recent information tells us that 2,500 Black people are gathered there. They have introduced the democratic institutions of America into the country of their forefathers. Liberia has a representative system of government, Black jurymen, Black magistrates, and Black priests; churches have been built, newspapers founded, and, by a strange reversal in the course of the world’s affairs, white men are forbidden to stay within the settlement. *u

t [ This society took the name “The Society for the Colonization of the Blacks.” See its annual reports, and especially the fifteenth. See also the pamphlet already mentioned, titled “Letters on the Colonization Society, and on its probable Results,” by Mr. Carey, Philadelphia, 1833.]

u [ The founders of the settlement laid down this last rule. They feared that a state of things might arise in Africa like the one on the frontiers of the United States, and that if Black people, like the Native Americans, were brought into collision with a people better educated than themselves, they would be destroyed before they could be civilized.]

This is indeed a strange caprice of fortune. Two hundred years have now passed since the people of Europe set out to tear the Black man from his family and his home in order to carry him to the shores of North America. Today the European settlers are busy sending the descendants of those same Black people back to the Continent from which they were first taken. The barbarous Africans have been brought into contact with civilization in the midst of bondage, and have become acquainted with free political institutions in slavery. Until now Africa has been closed to the arts and sciences of the whites; but perhaps the inventions of Europe will now penetrate those regions, since Africans themselves are introducing them. The settlement of Liberia is founded on a lofty and most fruitful idea; but whatever its results may be for the Continent of Africa, it can offer no remedy to the New World.

In twelve years the Colonization Society has transported 2,500 Black people to Africa; in the same period about 700,000 Black people were born in the United States. Suppose the colony of Liberia were situated so that it could receive thousands of new inhabitants every year, and suppose Black people were in a condition to be sent there with advantage. Suppose the Union gave the society annual subsidies *v and carried Black people to Africa in the vessels of the state. It would still be unable to offset the natural increase of the Black population. And since it could not remove in a year as many people as are born on its territory in the same time, it would fail to halt the growth of the evil, which increases daily in the States. *w The Black race will never leave those shores of the American continent to which it was brought by the passions and vices of Europeans, and it will not disappear from the New World as long as it continues to exist. The inhabitants of the United States may delay the calamities they fear, but they cannot now destroy their efficient cause.

v [ Nor would these be the only difficulties of the undertaking. If the Union set out to buy up the Black people now in America in order to transport them to Africa, the price of slaves, rising with their scarcity, would soon become enormous, and the Northern States would never agree to spend such great sums for a purpose that would bring them so little advantage. If the Union seized the slaves in the Southern States by force, or at a price fixed by law, insurmountable resistance would arise in that part of the country. Both alternatives are equally impossible.]

w [ In 1830 there were in the United States 2,010,327 slaves and 319,439 free Black people, 2,329,766 Black people in all, who formed about one-fifth of the total population of the United States at that time.]

I am obliged to confess that I do not regard the abolition of slavery as a means of warding off the struggle between the two races in the United States. Black people may remain slaves for a long time without complaining; but once they are raised to the level of free men, they will soon revolt at being deprived of all their civil rights, and since they cannot become the equals of the whites, they will soon declare themselves enemies. In the North everything helped to make emancipation easy, and slavery was abolished without putting free Black people in a position that could become formidable, since their number was too small for them ever to claim the exercise of their rights. But the South is different. For the slave-owners of the North, the question of slavery was a question of commerce and manufacturing; for those of the South it is a question of life and death. God forbid that I should try to justify the principle of the enslavement of Black people, as some American writers have done! I only observe that not all the countries that once adopted that execrable principle are equally able to abandon it at present.

When I consider the condition of the South, I can see only two courses open to the white inhabitants of those States: either to emancipate Black people and mingle with them, or, remaining separate from them, to keep them in slavery as long as possible. All intermediate measures seem to me likely to end, and soon, in the most horrible of civil wars, and perhaps in the extermination of one of the two races. This is how the Americans of the South view the question, and they act consistently with it. Since they are determined not to mingle with Black people, they refuse to emancipate them.

It is not that the people of the South regard slavery as necessary to the planter’s wealth. On this point many of them agree with their Northern countrymen in freely admitting that slavery is harmful to their interest. But they are convinced that, however harmful it may be, they hold their lives on no other terms. The education now spreading in the South has convinced the inhabitants that slavery is injurious to the slave-owner, but it has also shown them, more clearly than before, that there is no way of getting rid of its bad consequences. Hence arises a strange contrast: the more the usefulness of slavery is disputed, the more firmly it is established in the laws; and while the principle of servitude is gradually abolished in the North, that very principle gives rise to harsher and harsher consequences in the South.

The legislation of the Southern States concerning slaves presents today such unparalleled atrocities that they suffice to show how radically the laws of humanity have been perverted, and to reveal the desperate position of the community in which that legislation was enacted. The Americans of this part of the Union have not, indeed, increased the hardships of slavery; on the contrary, they have improved the physical condition of the slaves. The only means by which the ancients maintained slavery were fetters and death; the Americans of the South of the Union have discovered more intellectual safeguards for the duration of their power. They have turned their despotism and violence against the human mind. In antiquity, precautions were taken to keep the slave from breaking his chains; today measures are taken to deprive him even of the desire for freedom. The ancients held the bodies of their slaves in bondage, but they placed no restraint on the mind and no check on education; and they acted consistently with their established principle, since slavery then had a natural end, and one day or another the slave might be set free and become the equal of his master. But the Americans of the South, who do not admit that Black people can ever be blended with themselves, have forbidden them, under severe penalties, to be taught to read or write; and since they will not raise them to their own level, they push them down as nearly as possible to that of animals.

The slave had always been allowed the hope of liberty to lighten the hardships of his condition. But the Americans of the South are well aware that emancipation cannot fail to be dangerous when the freed man can never be assimilated to his former master. To give a man his freedom and leave him in wretchedness and disgrace is nothing less than to prepare a future leader of a slave revolt. Moreover, it has long been noticed that the presence of a free Black person vaguely disturbs the minds of his less fortunate brethren and gives them a dim idea of their rights. The Americans of the South have therefore taken measures to prevent slave-owners, in most cases, from emancipating their slaves — not, indeed, by a positive prohibition, but by subjecting that step to various formalities that are hard to satisfy. I happened to meet an old man in the South of the Union who had lived in an illicit relationship with one of his Black female slaves and had had several children by her, who were born the slaves of their father. He had indeed often thought of leaving them at least their liberty in his will; but years had passed without his being able to overcome the legal obstacles to their emancipation, and in the meantime old age had come and he was about to die. He pictured his sons dragged from market to market, passing from a parent’s authority to the rod of a stranger, until these horrible forebodings drove his dying imagination to frenzy. When I saw him he was a prey to all the anguish of despair, and he made me feel how awful is nature’s retribution on those who have broken her laws.

These evils are unquestionably great; but they are the necessary and foreseen consequence of the very principle of modern slavery. When the Europeans chose their slaves from a race different from their own, which many of them considered inferior to the other races of mankind, and which they all rejected with horror at any thought of intimate connection, they must have believed that slavery would last forever. For no intermediate state can be lasting between the excessive inequality produced by servitude and the complete equality that originates in independence. The Europeans did dimly feel this truth, but without acknowledging it even to themselves. Whenever they have had dealings with Black people, their conduct has been dictated either by their interest and pride or by their compassion. They first violated every right of humanity in their treatment of Black people, and afterward they informed them that those rights were precious and inviolable. They pretended to open their ranks to the slaves, but Black people who tried to enter the community were driven back with scorn; and they have been led, carelessly and unintentionally, to accept freedom in place of slavery, without having the courage to be either wholly wicked or wholly just.

If it is impossible to foresee a time when the Americans of the South will mingle their blood with that of Black people, can they let their slaves become free without endangering their own security? And if they are obliged to keep that race in bondage to save their own families, may they not be excused for using the means best suited to that end? The events taking place in the Southern States of the Union seem to me at once the most horrible and the most natural results of slavery. When I see the order of nature overturned, and when I hear the cry of humanity struggling in vain against the laws, my indignation does not fall on the men of our own time who are the instruments of these outrages. I reserve my execration for those who, after a thousand years of freedom, brought slavery back into the world once more.

Whatever efforts the Americans of the South make to maintain slavery, they will not always succeed. Slavery is now confined to a single region of the civilized earth; Christianity attacks it as unjust and political economy as harmful; and it now stands in contrast with democratic liberties and the knowledge of our age. It cannot survive. By the master’s choice or by the slave’s will, it will end; and in either case great calamities may be expected to follow. If liberty is refused to the Black people of the South, they will in the end seize it by force; if it is given, they will before long abuse it. *x

x [ [This chapter no longer applies to the condition of the Black race in the United States, since the abolition of slavery was the result, though not the aim, of the great Civil War, and Black people have been raised to the condition not only of freedmen but of citizens; and in some States they hold preponderating political power because they are the numerical majority. Thus in South Carolina there were in 1870, 289,667 whites and 415,814 Black people. But the emancipation of the slaves has not solved the problem of how two races so different and so hostile are to live together in peace in one country on equal terms. That problem is as difficult as ever, perhaps more so; and the author’s remarks still apply perfectly to this difficulty.]]
What Are the Chances in Favor of the Duration of the American Union, and What Dangers Threaten It *y

y [ [This chapter is one of the most curious and interesting parts of the work, because it takes in almost all the constitutional and social questions raised by the great secession of the South and decided by the outcome of the Civil War. But it must be admitted that the author’s sagacity is sometimes at fault in these speculations, and did not save him from considerable errors, which the course of events has since made apparent. He held that “the legislators of the Constitution of 1789 were not appointed to constitute the government of a single people, but to regulate the association of several States; that the Union was formed by the voluntary agreement of the States, and in uniting together they have not forfeited their nationality, nor have they been reduced to the condition of one and the same people.” From this he inferred that “if one of the States chose to withdraw its name from the contract, it would be difficult to disprove its right of doing so; and that the Federal Government would have no means of maintaining its claims directly, either by force or by right.” This is the Southern theory of the Constitution, and the whole case of the South in favor of secession. To many Europeans, and to some American (Northern) jurists, this view appeared sound; but the North resisted it vigorously, and it was crushed by force of arms.

The author of this book was mistaken in supposing that the “Union was a vast body which presents no definite object to patriotic feeling.” When the day of trial came, millions of men were ready to lay down their lives for it. He was also mistaken in supposing that the Federal Executive is so weak that it needs the free consent of the governed to survive, and that it would be defeated in a struggle to maintain the Union against one or more separate States. In 1861 nine States, with a population of 8,753,000, seceded and carried on for four years a resolute but unequal contest for independence, but they were defeated.

Lastly, the author was mistaken in supposing that a community of interests would always prevail between North and South, strong enough to bind them together. He overlooked the influence that the question of slavery was bound to have on the Union the moment the majority of the people of the North declared against it. In 1831, when the author visited America, the anti-slavery agitation had scarcely begun, and the fact of Southern slavery was accepted by men of all parties, even in the States where there were no slaves. That was unquestionably the view taken by all the States and by all American statesmen at the time the Constitution was adopted in 1789. But in the course of thirty years a great change took place, and the North refused to perpetuate what had become the “peculiar institution” of the South, especially since it gave the South a kind of aristocratic preponderance. The result was the ratification, in December 1865, of the celebrated 13th article or amendment of the Constitution, which declared that “neither slavery nor involuntary servitude — except as a punishment for crime — shall exist within the United States.” Soon afterward the 15th article was added: “The right of citizens to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States, or by any State, on account of race, color, or previous servitude.” The emancipation of several million Black slaves without compensation, and the transfer to them of political preponderance in the States where they outnumber the white population, were acts of the North totally opposed to the interests of the South, and could only have been carried out by conquest. — Translator’s Note.]]

Why the Preponderating Force Lies in the States Rather Than in the Union — The Union will last only as long as all the States choose to belong to it — Causes that tend to keep them united — Usefulness of the Union in resisting foreign enemies and in preventing the presence of foreigners in America — No natural barriers between the several States — No conflicting interests to divide them — Reciprocal interests of the Northern, Southern, and Western States — Intellectual ties of union — Uniformity of opinions — Dangers to the Union resulting from the different characters and passions of its citizens — Character of the citizens in the South and in the North — The rapid growth of the Union one of its greatest dangers — Progress of the population to the Northwest — Power gravitates in the same direction — Passions originating in sudden turns of fortune — Whether the existing government of the Union tends to gain strength or to lose it — Various signs of its decrease — Internal improvements — Waste lands — Native Americans — The Bank — The Tariff — General Jackson.

The survival of the existing institutions of the several States depends to some extent on the survival of the Union itself. It is therefore important to begin by inquiring into the probable fate of the Union. One point may indeed be assumed at once: if the present confederation were dissolved, it seems to me beyond dispute that the States now composing it would not return to their original isolated condition, but that several unions would then be formed in place of one. I do not intend to inquire into the principles on which these new unions would probably be established, but only to show what causes may bring about the breakup of the existing confederation.

For this purpose I shall have to retrace some of the steps I have already taken and return to topics I have discussed before. I know the reader may accuse me of repetition, but the importance of the matter still to be treated is my excuse. I would rather say too much than too little to be fully understood, and I prefer to harm the author rather than slight the subject.

The legislators who framed the Constitution of 1789 tried to give the federal power a distinct and preponderating authority. But they were limited by the nature of the task they had undertaken. They were not appointed to constitute the government of a single people, but to regulate the association of several States; and whatever their inclinations might be, they could not avoid dividing the exercise of sovereignty in the end.

To understand the consequences of this division, it is necessary to draw a short distinction among the affairs of government. Some matters are national by their very nature; that is, they affect the nation as a body and can be entrusted only to the man or the assembly of men who most completely represent the entire nation. War and diplomacy may be counted among these. Other matters are provincial by their very nature; that is, they affect only certain localities and can be handled properly only in that locality. The budget of a municipality is an example. Lastly, there are certain matters of a mixed nature, which are national in that they affect all the citizens who make up the nation, and provincial in that the nation itself need not provide for all of them. Such are the rights that regulate the civil and political condition of the citizens. No society can exist without civil and political rights. These rights therefore concern all citizens alike; but it is not always necessary to the existence and prosperity of the nation that these rights be uniform, nor, consequently, that the central authority regulate them.

There are, then, two distinct categories of matters placed under the direction of the sovereign power, and these categories are found in all well-constituted communities, whatever the basis of the political constitution may otherwise be. Between these two extremes lie the matters I have called mixed. Since these matters are neither exclusively national nor entirely provincial, they may be handled by a national or by a provincial government, according to the agreement of the contracting parties, without in any way impairing the contract of association.

The sovereign power is usually formed by the union of separate individuals who make up a people; and individual powers or collective forces, each representing a very small portion of the sovereign authority, are the only elements subject to the general government of their choice. In this case the general government is more naturally called upon to regulate not only the affairs of essential national importance but also those of more local interest, and the local governments are reduced to the small share of sovereign authority indispensable to their prosperity.

But sometimes the sovereign authority is composed of political bodies already organized, by virtue of circumstances that predate their union. In this case the provincial governments take control not only of the affairs that more particularly belong to their province, but of all or part of the mixed affairs mentioned above. For the confederate nations, which were independent sovereign States before their union and still represent a very considerable share of the sovereign power, have consented to cede to the general government only the exercise of those rights indispensable to the Union.

When the national government, besides the prerogatives inherent in its nature, is invested with the right to regulate affairs that relate partly to general and partly to local interests, it has a preponderating influence. Not only are its own rights extensive, but all the rights it does not hold exist only by its sufferance, and it may be feared that its influence will deprive the provincial governments of their natural and necessary prerogatives.
